subject: history
title: The Troubles in Northern Ireland 1968-1998
welcome_lead: From Bloody Sunday to the Good Friday Agreement, study three decades of conflict and peacemaking in Northern Ireland.
meta_desc: IBDP History Rights & Protest Adventure 3: Northern Ireland Troubles 1968-1998 and the Good Friday Agreement.
final_note: You have followed a hard-won peace. Power-sharing remains a sensitive achievement requiring sustained effort.

concepts.def: Late-1960s movement led by NICRA campaigning against discrimination against Catholics.
Killing of 13 civilians by British paratroopers during a civil rights march in Derry on 30 January 1972.
Republican paramilitary group formed in 1969 committed to ending British rule in Northern Ireland.
Groups such as the UVF and UDA committed to maintaining union with Britain.
Republican prisoners' protest for political status during which Bobby Sands and nine others died.
Multi-party peace accord of 10 April 1998 establishing power-sharing and consent principle.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA) modelled itself on the US movement, demanding an end to discrimination in housing, voting and policing. Confrontations between marchers and loyalists/police escalated in 1968-69, leading to the deployment of the British army in August 1969 and the formation of the Provisional IRA.

walkthroughs.h2: From Bloody Sunday to hunger strikes
walkthroughs.body_html: The 1970s witnessed internment without trial (1971), Bloody Sunday (30 January 1972), direct rule from Westminster and an escalating campaign of bombings and shootings by republican and loyalist paramilitaries. The 1981 hunger strikes, in which Bobby Sands and nine other prisoners died, deepened polarisation but also propelled Sinn Féin into electoral politics.

The Anglo-Irish Agreement (1985), Hume-Adams talks, IRA and loyalist ceasefires of 1994 and the Mitchell Principles paved the way for negotiations. The Good Friday/Belfast Agreement of 10 April 1998 created a power-sharing Assembly, North-South and British-Irish institutions and accepted that change in Northern Ireland's status required majority consent.
